content: Electroplating is a process that involves the use of electrical current to reduce cations of a specific material from a solution and deposit a thin layer of that material, often a metal, onto a conductive object. This technique is employed to enhance properties such as abrasion resistance, wear resistance, corrosion protection, lubricity, and aesthetic qualities on surfaces that otherwise lack these characteristics. Additionally, electroplating can be used to increase the thickness of undersized parts. The process of electroplating is referred to as electrodeposition, which operates in a manner analogous to a galvanic cell but in reverse. The object to be plated serves as the cathode in the circuit. In one common method, the anode is composed of the metal intended for deposition onto the cathode. Both the anode and cathode are immersed in an electrolyte solution containing dissolved metal salts and other ions that facilitate the flow of electricity. A rectifier provides direct current to the cathode, causing the metal ions in the electrolyte to lose their charge and deposit onto the cathode. Simultaneously, the anode dissolves gradually, replenishing the metal ions in the solution. In some cases, a non-consumable anode, such as lead, is used, and the metal ions in the bath must be periodically replenished as they are depleted. In the electroplating cell, the anode and cathode are connected to an external direct current power supply, typically a rectifier. The anode is connected to the positive terminal, while the cathode (the object to be plated) is connected to the negative terminal. When the power supply is activated, the metal at the anode undergoes oxidation, transitioning from a zero-valence state to positively charged cations. These cations combine with anions in the solution and are subsequently reduced at the cathode, depositing as a metallic layer in their zero-valence state. For example, in an acidic solution, copper from the anode is oxidized to Cu²⁺ by losing two electrons. The Cu²⁺ ions associate with sulfate anions (SO₄²⁻) in the solution to form copper sulfate. At the cathode, the Cu²⁺ ions are reduced to metallic copper by gaining two electrons, effectively transferring copper from the anode to the cathode. Electroplating typically involves the deposition of a single metallic element rather than an alloy, although certain alloys, such as brass and solder, can also be electrodeposited. In some cases, free cyanides (e.g., potassium cyanide) are added to the electrolyte to facilitate anode corrosion, maintain a consistent metal ion concentration, and enhance conductivity. Non-metallic chemicals, such as carbonates and phosphates, may also be added to improve conductivity. When plating is not desired on specific areas, stop-offs like tape, foil, lacquers, or waxes are applied to prevent the electrolyte from contacting those regions. A preliminary plating process known as striking is often used to achieve a thin, high-quality, and well-adhered initial layer (approximately 1 micrometer thick) on the substrate. This serves as a foundation for subsequent plating processes. Striking involves a high current density and a bath with a low ion concentration. Although the process is slow, it ensures good adhesion and is particularly useful when plating metals with poor adhesion to the substrate. For example, a copper strike may be applied to zinc alloys before nickel plating to improve adhesion. The current density, defined as the amperage of the electroplating current divided by the surface area of the part, significantly influences the deposition rate, plating adhesion, and overall quality. Higher current densities result in faster deposition rates but may lead to poor adhesion and plating quality if the rate is excessively high. Some plating cells use a pulsed current cycle (e.g., 8–15 seconds on, followed by 1–3 seconds off) to allow high current densities while maintaining plating quality. In certain cases, the current is reversed to address uneven plating rates, redistributing material from thicker sections to thinner areas, effectively leveling the surface. Brush electroplating is a related technique used for localized plating or plating entire items using a brush saturated with plating solution. The brush, typically made of stainless steel wrapped in a cloth material, acts as the anode and is connected to the positive terminal of a low-voltage direct current power source. The item to be plated is connected to the negative terminal. The operator applies the plating solution with the brush, moving it continuously to ensure even distribution. Brush electroplating offers advantages such as portability, minimal masking requirements, and low solution volume requirements. However, it requires greater operator involvement and may not achieve the same plate thickness as tank plating. Electroless deposition, in contrast to electroplating, does not require an external electrical current. Instead, it relies on a chemical reducing agent in the solution to facilitate the deposition of metal onto the substrate. For example, electroless nickel plating is a common application of this process. Cleanliness is critical for successful electroplating, as even molecular layers of oil can prevent proper adhesion of the coating. ASTM B322 provides guidelines for cleaning metals prior to electroplating. Cleaning methods include solvent cleaning, hot alkaline detergent cleaning, electrocleaning, and acid etching. The water break test is a common industrial method for assessing cleanliness. In this test, a clean metal surface retains an unbroken sheet of water, while hydrophobic contaminants cause the water to bead and drain rapidly. Modern electrochemistry, which underpins electroplating, was pioneered by Luigi V. Brugnatelli in 1805. Using Alessandro Volta's voltaic pile, Brugnatelli conducted the first electrodeposition experiments. However, his work was suppressed by the French Academy of Sciences and did not gain widespread industrial use until the 1830s. By 1839, scientists in Britain and Russia independently developed similar processes for copper electroplating. In 1840, John Wright discovered that potassium cyanide was a suitable electrolyte for gold and silver electroplating. His associates, George and Henry Elkington, were awarded the first patents for electroplating and established the industry in Birmingham, England. As electrochemistry advanced, the relationship between the science and the electroplating process became better understood, leading to the development of non-decorative metal plating processes. By the 1850s, commercial electroplating of nickel, brass, tin, and zinc was established. The advent of electric generators in the late 19th century enabled higher currents, facilitating the bulk processing of machine components, hardware, and automotive parts requiring corrosion protection and enhanced wear properties. The two World Wars and the aviation industry's growth spurred further advancements, including hard chromium plating, bronze alloy plating, and sulfamate nickel plating. Electroplating equipment evolved from manually operated wooden tanks to automated systems capable of processing large quantities of parts efficiently. One notable development in electroplating was the work of American physicist Richard Feynman, who contributed to the technology for plating metal onto plastic. This innovation allowed for the fulfillment of commercial promises and expanded the applications of electroplating. Today, electroplating is a critical component of the LIGA process used in the manufacture of MEMS devices.
